utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Civil Service and Labor.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

chapters.summary: Chair Shirley Aldebol welcomes attendees, identifies herself, and states the hearing topic: municipal recruitment and pathways to civil service.
chapters.title: Chair Aldebol opens hearing on municipal recruitment and civil service pathways

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to today's hearing of the New York City Council's Committee on Civil Service and Labor.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Shirley Aldeball, Chair of this committee.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Today we will be discussing municipal recruitment and pathways to civil service.

chapters.summary: Aldebol recalls the April hearing on rebuilding the municipal workforce and outlines current DCAS programs like the Civil Service Pathways Fellowship and Public Service Core Program.
chapters.title: Chair Aldebol reviews prior hearing and existing recruitment programs

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: In April, this committee held a hearing on rebuilding the municipal workforce, where we discussed the new administration's hiring strategies and heard from DCAS Commissioner Kitase about how the new administration planned to advance the municipal workforce.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: These discussions touched on several different strategies to expand pathways into civil service.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Currently, the administration operates several programs aimed at recruiting talented candidates to serve the city they love and ensuring that they are equipped with the information they need to successfully find a position that suits their skills.

chapters.summary: She describes the Fellowship for recent graduates and the Public Service Core Program for interns, emphasizing equity and representation.
chapters.title: Chair Aldebol details Civil Service Pathways Fellowship and Public Service Core

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The Civil Service Pathways Fellowship, which is administered by DCAS in partnership with CUNY,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: focuses on recent graduates and offers participants a two-year full-time job with city agencies and a chance to take civil service exam after the first year of completed service.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: DCAS also offers the Public Service Core Program, which facilitates internships with the administration through a work-study program for applicants who are currently in their undergraduate or graduate degree programs.

chapters.summary: Aldebol notes outreach events, the Civil Service Ambassador Program, and the Office of Citywide Recruitment's partnerships with educational and community organizations.
chapters.title: Chair Aldebol highlights outreach and Civil Service Ambassador Program

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: These initiatives are

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: offered alongside regular outreach and recruitment events through the Civil Service Ambassador Program.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: These programs are designed to provide applicants with the skills and information needed to navigate the application process into the municipal workforce, with particular emphasis on increasing equity and representation within civil service.

chapters.summary: She mentions 308 outreach events in FY2025 and expanded outreach to foster care and juvenile justice facilities.
chapters.title: Chair Aldebol discusses Office of Citywide Recruitment and outreach expansion

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: DCAS also has a dedicated office of citywide recruitment, which is tasked with building partnerships with educational, institutional, and community-based organizations to promote city government jobs.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: These efforts are reflected in the 308 outreach events that OCR participated in fiscal year 2025 that were conducted across the city.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Furthermore, we want to highlight that OCR has recently expanded the types of pathways at which they are holding these events, including increased outreach at foster care programs and juvenile justice facilities.

chapters.summary: Aldebol cites nearly 5% overall vacancy rate, with DSS at 15% and Human Rights Commission at 20%.
chapters.title: Chair Aldebol notes persistent vacancy rates across agencies

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yet, despite these efforts, the city still has a vacancy rate of nearly 5% overall, with some agencies seeing vacancy rates in the double digits.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The Department of Social Services, for example, whose staff support some of our most vulnerable New Yorkers, has a vacancy rate of almost 15%.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And the Human Rights Commission has a vacancy rate of nearly 20%.

chapters.summary: She notes hiring delays over a year, non-competitive salaries, and limited upskilling, making civil service unattractive.
chapters.title: Chair Aldebol addresses hiring delays and challenges for candidates

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Civil service vacancies have remained persistent, and we have heard from municipal workers,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: representatives and advocates that hiring delays can take over a year.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: When that timeline is paired with non-competitive salaries, inconsistent training, and limited upskilling opportunities, the civil service becomes unattractive to many highly qualified potential employees.

chapters.summary: Aldebol states the committee will conduct oversight on outreach, youth apprenticeship, and plans for a fully staffed workforce.
chapters.title: Chair Aldebol outlines committee's oversight goals and commitment

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Moreover, while we understand that these existing timelines mean that the new administration's expanded strategies will not show measurable results yet,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: we are committed to ensuring that the policies being implemented today will only serve to improve the civil service process of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: This committee looks forward to conducting oversight on the department's required outreach and recruitment, ask about how new initiatives such as the youth apprenticeship title,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: and delve into how this administration plans to focus its efforts to ensure a fully staffed municipal workforce.

chapters.summary: She thanks committee staff, her chief of staff, and recognizes Council Members Morano and Hudson.
chapters.title: Chair Aldebol thanks staff and recognizes attending council members

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Before we begin, I'd like to thank committee staff, Senior Policy Analyst Nina Rosenberg, and Senior Legislative Counsel Rie Ogasuara for their hard work in preparing this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank my Chief of Staff, Sophia Brown, and my District 13 team for the work that you do to serve the Bronxite District 13 constituents.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: At this point, I would like to recognize that we've been joined by council members Frank Marano and Crystal Hudson.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I will now hear testimony from representatives of DCAS, and I'll turn to committee counsel to administer the oath for this panel.

chapters.title: Committee counsel administers affirmation to DCAS panel

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We will now hear testimony from the administration.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Before we begin, I will administer the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Planelists, please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I will read the affirmation once, then call on each of you individually to respond.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee, and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner Porter?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Commissioner Uttar?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Katrina Porter introduces herself and Katie Ann Otar, thanks the committee, and begins discussing DCAS career pathway programs.
chapters.title: Deputy Commissioner Porter introduces DCAS panel and thanks committee

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Aldebar and members of the City Council's Committee on Civil Service and Labor.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: My name is Katrina Porter, and I proudly serve as Deputy Commissioner and Chief Human Capital Officer for the Department of Citywide Administrative Services, more commonly known as DCAS.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: I am joined today by my colleague, Katie Ann Otar, Assistant Commissioner for Workforce Operations at DCAS.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We are grateful for the opportunity to be here with you today to discuss the Vital City Civil Service Career Pathway programs overseen by our agency.

chapters.summary: Porter describes the range of programs from entry-level to specialized professionals, all aimed at bringing top talent into city agencies.
chapters.title: Porter outlines DCAS career pathway programs and shared goals

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Each program has its own distinct qualities, but together they create pathways into public service for a wide range of talent, from those just beginning their careers to those looking to advance and grow,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: as well as professionals with highly specialized skills and expertise.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: What connects them all is a shared interest in serving government and making a difference for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Together, these programs are part of our broader efforts to bring top talent into city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And most importantly, offer New Yorkers opportunities to build meaningful, long-term, and life-changing careers in public service.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: To achieve this, DCAS supports agencies by

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: employing strategic, targeted, and ongoing recruitment efforts, as well as creating spaces and forums for professional development.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It gives us great pride to say that DCAS is often there for municipal staff from their very first government application to their first day of work, all the way through to the day they retire.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We also share the council's interest in ensuring that there are ample pipelines into city service and that those pathways are strong, robust, and continue to evolve to meet the ever-changing workforce landscape.

chapters.summary: Starting July 1, 2026, exams are free for NYC high school students and first-time test takers, as part of Local Law 57 compliance.
chapters.title: Porter announces free civil service exams for high school students and first-time test takers

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Recognizing how the way people find, access, and engage with information has changed, and we've invested in new ways to make civil service more accessible.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Starting this past July 1st, 2026, civil service exams are now free for New York City high school students and first-time test takers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: This includes all of the city's students, those attending a public school, private school, charter school, parochial school, or home school.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: This has also afforded us an opportunity to potentially reach millions of first-time test takers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: This initiative was undertaken as part of our compliance with Local Law 57 of 2005, illustrates what we can achieve when government works together.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It is as much a win for us as it is for the council, and we are grateful for the partnership.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Coupled with our existing fee waivers, DCO

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: CAS is working to ensure that financial barriers do not stop a prospective candidate from applying and taking an exam.

chapters.summary: DCAS now offers exam notices in any language and distributes brochures to CUNY students to demystify civil service.
chapters.title: Porter highlights translated exam notices and CUNY brochures

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In addition, this past July, we rolled out a new update that allowed notices of examination to be translated into any language a candidate is most comfortable with.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We would like to recognize Councilmember Carmen De La Rosa for this idea, and we are very excited to see how translatable notices of exams can remove limitations to accessing information about civil service opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: As part of our compliance with Local Law 191 of 2005, DCAS has also begun producing and distributing brochures to CUNY for prospective, current, and recent

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: graduated students designed to demystify the civil service system and provide easily digestible information on how to get a job in city government.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: With hundreds of thousands of students across the city, this is another vital touchpoint to recruit for municipal service.

chapters.summary: The two-year fellowship for CUNY graduates has expanded to 400 fellows and a second yearly cohort, with 75% transitioning to full-time jobs.
chapters.title: Porter details Civil Service Pathway Fellowship and its expansion

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Now I'd like to talk more about our marquee programs at DCAS.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Civil Service Pathway Fellowship, the Urban Fellows Program, the Public Service Corps, Summer Internship Program, and 55A.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The Civil Service Pathway Fellowship is a two-year program for City University of New York graduates designed to create a pipeline from college to a career in civil service.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The fellowship is full-time and

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: offers competitive salary and benefits for graduates.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Perhaps most importantly, fellows receive professional development training and experience that helps them to qualify for various civil service exams after completing the first year of the program.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: After completing the program, fellows can transition into a full-time position within their agency.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The Civil Service Pathway Fellowship serves as a critical component of our talent pipeline.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We recruit interested college and graduate students for seven different career tracks through our program, which helps agencies and mayoral offices fill critical service roles.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Just this past August, we announced a major expansion to this program, increasing it to 400 fellows up from the prior 200, doubling the reach of the program,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: and creating a second yearly cohort, creating even more opportunities for recent graduates to join.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: This program has been nothing short of successful, with approximately 75% of graduates transitioning to full-time jobs from the program.

chapters.summary: The Public Service Corps, celebrating 60 years, hosts 120 interns across 13 agencies; the Summer Internship Program hired over 900 interns across 27 agencies.
chapters.title: Porter describes Public Service Corps and Summer Internship Program

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Another program we administer is the New York City Public Service Corps, the nation's first and largest off-campus internship program

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: that connects undergraduate and graduate students who participate in federal work study with paid or academic credit internships across a range of city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: DCAS partners with New York City colleges, universities, and city agencies to offer diverse internship experiences that expose

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: all students to public service careers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Celebrating its 60th year this year, Public Service Corps provides interns with crucial experience to help set them up on a path to public service.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: This year, 13 agency partners are hosting more than 120 Public Service Corps interns.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: This program is a tremendously beneficial one and has seen many city leaders come through the program.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: I would also like to highlight two shorter-term programs that we oversee.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The first is the Summer Internship Program, which provides graduate and undergraduate students and recent graduates with valuable experience working for city government.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Interns work on meaningful projects, build professional skills, and explore career opportunities across a wide range of city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Interns can work during the summer from May through September for a maximum of 13 weeks.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: This year, over 900 interns were hired across 27 agencies.

chapters.summary: The Urban Fellows Program is a nine-month fellowship with 77% staying on last year; the 55A program allows hiring of qualified persons with disabilities without an exam.
chapters.title: Porter discusses Urban Fellows Program and 55A program

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The second of our shorter-term programs is the Urban Fellows Program, a nine-month fellowship that combines work in mayoral offices and city agencies with volunteer service opportunities

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: and a weekly seminar series that explores current urban issues impacting public policy.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Urban fellows are placed at an array of agencies across the city where they learn about public policy through a hands-on approach.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We continue to see a growing number of fellows remain in city government.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: with 77% staying on last year and 38% staying on this year.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The last pathway I would like to speak on is our 55A program, a valuable asset in our recruitment portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Our administration of the 55A program allows a qualified person with a certified mental or physical disability to be hired into competitive civil service positions without having to take an exam.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: As stated earlier, most City of New York jobs require the candidates to take and pass a competitive civil service exam before they can be hired.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Through our 55A program, eligible persons are evaluated for positions based on their qualifications and interviews.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: This program is a great equalizer for municipal hiring and promotes city work in an equitable manner for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Currently, we are working closely with the Mayor's Office of People with Disabilities to amplify its reach.

chapters.summary: Over 80% of city positions require an exam; DCAS administers 200+ exams yearly and offers the Bridge Exam for multiple positions with one fee.
chapters.title: Porter emphasizes civil service exams and Bridge Exam

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In tandem with our marquee recruitment programs, civil service exams continue to be the most important pathway into city jobs.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Exams are the most well-known facets of DCAS's work to promote municipal work to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: More than 80% of city government positions require a civil service test, and it is the most critical pathway to service that we oversee.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Each year, DCAS typically administers more than 200 exams.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Administering exams is one thing, making sure New York is no

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: about those opportunities, understand the process, and can easily take the next step is another.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: That is why we take every opportunity to broaden the conversation around civil service exams and the benefits of a career with the city.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We are expanding our outreach across media channels, developing thoughtful, strategic social media content designed to demystify civil service and meeting New Yorkers where they are.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And we are also finding ways to make the exam process more accessible and streamlined, evidenced by innovations like the New York City Bridge Exam.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: With the New York City Bridge Exam, candidates pay one fee, take one exam, and become eligible for multiple positions.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In its fifth year of administration, bridge exams are removing barriers and making the path into public service a far more efficient process for New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: The Office of Citywide Recruitment meets New Yorkers across all boroughs through hiring halls, career fairs, and Civil Service 101 presentations.
chapters.title: Porter details Office of Citywide Recruitment and outreach efforts

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: As for recruitment, our Office of Citywide Recruitment is focused on meeting New Yorkers where they are, across all five boroughs, and at every stage of their career journey.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: You will find DCAS representatives at New York City jobs hiring halls, at career fairs, and in communities connecting directly with New Yorkers looking for work.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We also partner with city agencies to host title-specific hiring events that help address their immediate workforce needs.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: These efforts connect with New Yorkers where they are, and I'm proud to say that we have engaged tens of thousands of prospective candidates across the five boroughs through these programs.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Our work isn't just about filling jobs.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We are also invested in helping New Yorkers understand how they can build a career in public service.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Throughout each year, we host civil service 101 presentations at New York City public schools, higher education institutions, with community-based organizations, and at faith-based institutions across the city,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: providing practical information about how to navigate the civil service process and explore opportunities in municipal government.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We also look to connect to a wide range of audiences through multiple mediums, from direct person-to-person engagement to social media and press outreach.

chapters.summary: The NYC Jobs newsletter reaches 250,000 people; social media impressions are up 251%, interactions up 329%, and video views up 408%.
chapters.title: Porter highlights newsletters, social media growth, and digital strategy

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We take a comprehensive approach to promote civil service.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In addition, we also publish the New York City Jobs newsletter and send out monthly e-blasts to get the word out to hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers about career opportunities in municipal government.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In addition to the efforts undertaken at the agency level.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: With the monthly New York City Jobs newsletter alone, we reach more than 250,000 New Yorkers looking for work.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Beyond, we also manage and maintain New York City's job website.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In 2025, the New York City Jobs website received over 1.8 million applications.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: When it comes to social media, we are currently expanding our presence online and looking to more generally utilize this important touch point.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: As per our last analysis, our average reach

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: across our social media channel is north of 460,000 impressions and growing.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: When it comes to social media, we are executing a highly intentional data-driven strategy to maximize this critical touchpoint.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Rather than simply expanding our presence, we have actively shifted our focus to authentic storytelling, short-form video, and real-time community engagement.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: As a result of this approach, our latest analysis for the month of August shows our cumulative reach across our social media channels.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Channels has surged to over 460,000 impressions, a massive 251% increase year over year.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Additionally, the strategic pivot has skyrocketed our total audience interactions by 329% and our video views by 408%.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Proving that our streamlined operations are deeply resonating with New Yorkers and rapidly growing our digital community.

chapters.summary: Porter concludes by emphasizing DCAS's commitment to making civil service faster and more transparent, and offers to answer questions.
chapters.title: Porter concludes testimony and offers to answer questions

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In conclusion, at DCAS, we are passionate about helping New Yorkers join civil service, and we are working tirelessly to position the city of New York as an employer of choice.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The civil service system unquestionably provides a pathway to the middle class for underserved and underrepresented communities.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Through the initiatives, programs, apprenticeships, and partnerships we've detailed here, DCAS has continued to expand access to government jobs.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: As we look ahead, please know that we

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We are actively enacting strategic plans that will make our civil service system faster, more transparent, and aligned with the 21st century workforce and the city's operational needs.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and attention, and I'm happy now to answer any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I want to recognize Councilmember Caban, who is online.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm going to, rather than me start asking questions, because I have a lot of questions to ask, I'm going to turn it over to my colleagues first.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You know, this is like odd, right?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Because I know there are other hearings going on, and I want you to have an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm here for the long haul, so I'm going to turn it over first to Council Member Morano to ask.

chapters.summary: Morano thanks the chair, notes his role on Veterans Committee, and asks what DCAS is doing to recruit veterans beyond referring them to a website.
chapters.title: Morano thanks chair and begins questioning on veteran recruitment

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I appreciate the consideration.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I think every council member has the experience of being in a hearing for 20, 30, 40 minutes without being able to ask a single question because the chair chooses to ask so many of those questions.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So thank you for the consideration as well.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Commissioner, for your testimony as well.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to begin with our veterans.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I have the privilege of serving.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm being asked the Veterans Committee Chair, so it's an issue that I'm particularly interested in.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony discusses several recruitment programs, but I'd like to know what we're doing specifically to recruit veterans into city government.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We know veterans can use VetConnect NYC to access different employment services, but the Comptroller's Report recently raised some concerns about that portal.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What is DCAS doing to recruit veterans simply beyond referring them to a website?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And so first and foremost, we work very closely with our sister agency, you know, the Department of Veterans Affairs, to share information about upcoming examinations and, you know, information that would help

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: attract veterans into the city's workforce.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In addition, as it relates to our examination program, veterans are also, you know,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: eligible to take to claim, you know, special credits and fee waivers to help remove any barriers into the civil service system.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: I would also mention that we most recently participated in an event with the Department of Veterans Affairs to share information about civil service.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Our Office of Citywide Recruitment attended and we were there, you know, to share information about

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: the civil service system in general, examinations and other services that may be available to veterans who are looking to join the

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: the system.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So, you know, in general, we do share that information broadly with our sister agency.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Kaden, I don't know if you want to add anything else.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We do engage communities that work specifically with veterans.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So across the years, we try to develop relationships specifically with those organizations.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We also try to work with schools who have veteran-specific offices and to share the information about civil service, to go into more details about the veteran fee waivers that folks are able to get, the spouse fee waivers,

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: and also going into more details about what it means to qualify for the veterans credit.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So we also have those individuals on our mailing list who's getting our newsletters on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: There's always opportunities to increase our outreach to those communities, but we definitely make a dedicated effort to reach that community.

chapters.summary: Morano asks how many of the 1.8 million applications resulted in jobs; Porter says about 20,000 positions were filled, mostly interview-based.
chapters.title: Morano asks about NYC Jobs website applications and hires

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: A couple of quick non-veterans related questions.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony says the NYC Jobs website received more than 1.8 million applications last year.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's an enormous number.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many of those 1.8 million applications actually resulted in someone getting a job?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do you track that number?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: For 2025, it was about a little over 20,000 positions were filled through the jobs website.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And, you know, those are positions that do not require a civil service exam.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It's interview-based hiring.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But, yeah, that's the number, about 20,000.

chapters.summary: Morano asks how many applications were for positions without funding; Porter says posted positions are approved to be filled but will get back with concrete numbers.
chapters.title: Morano asks about unfunded positions on jobs website

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: One of the things that came up in the...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: the recent budget battle is the battle over positions that we might be paying for or which might be called for in the budget but aren't necessarily filled.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many of the applications that you guys received were submitted for positions that agencies did not yet have the approval or funding to fill?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: That's a good question.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We would have to get back to you to give you a concrete number.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But in general, positions that are posted on the jobs website are approved to be filled.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Gotcha.

chapters.summary: Morano questions whether the impressive social media growth translates to hires; Porter says it's too early to correlate but it's a step in the right direction.
chapters.title: Morano asks about social media metrics and hires

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I noticed something interesting towards the end of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You report that your social media impressions are up 251%.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We'll have to chat privately so you can give me some tips.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Audience interactions are up 329%, and video views are up 408%.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Those are...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Remarkably impressive.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But how many additional people actually got hired because of those campaigns?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Are you measuring that?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Because I don't necessarily think the public should judge a recruitment program by how many people watch the video.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We should judge it, obviously, by whether they found jobs or not.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So first, I'll say that those numbers are directly contributed to our commissioner's commitment to getting out information about city jobs and, you know, demystifying how to engage with the system.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: What I will say is that it may be a little bit too early to kind of correlate.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: that are actually getting jobs to the information that we're posting on social media.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: However, I think that it's an amazing step in the right direction to, you know, just continue to share information about the good jobs that are available.

chapters.summary: Morano notes only seven ambassador events on Staten Island and asks how many Staten Islanders were hired; Porter says they will check and that events focus on information sharing.
chapters.title: Morano asks about Staten Island outreach events and hires

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: One final question, if I may, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: According to the council's briefing paper, DCAS held 178 qualifying civil service ambassador events in fiscal year 2025.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Only seven were on Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony says you're meeting New Yorkers where they are, across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many Staten Islanders actually got hired as a result of those seven events?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We would have to check and see if we can get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But the main focus of these events is to share information about the system, not so much to tout a specific job or position.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The goal is to help folks understand how to engage with us and where to go for information in the event that they are looking for a particular job.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And, Kaden, I don't know if you want to add anything else.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Council Member Hudson?

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about the drop from 77% to 38% retention in the Urban Fellows Program; Otar explains the program year and factors like vacancies and candidate interest.
chapters.title: Hudson questions DCAS on Urban Fellows retention rates

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair, and hello, Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: One question I had from your testimony was you said we continue to see a growing number of fellows remaining in city government.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: This was specifically about the Urban Fellows Program.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: With 77% staying on last year and 38% staying on this year, which years...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Can those numbers be attributed to specifically calendar years, fiscal years?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So that'll be for the program year.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So our Urban Fellow program year usually starts from the, let's say this year we have a new group that starts from 2026, so they'll go into 2027.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So for the 38%, it was from 2025 to 2026.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And then for the 78%, it was from 2024 into 2025.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So they run from September to June.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: September to August.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We have some people that may stay on until August, yes.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, I'm just trying to figure out why there was such a drop, and if the year that you're referring to the 38% is completed, or if this is a partial number.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So it's completed.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: There are several factors that ties into whether or not individuals are able to stay on.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: As we mentioned, it's a nine-month program.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And so we do a couple of things in order to keep folks that are engaged and interested in city government.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We also know that individuals that participate in the program, they may relocate from a different city or state to participate.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And so it also depends on the opportunities that are available to them.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So we know that for the 78%, which was for the previous program.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You said 24 is 25.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And sorry, I didn't catch the nine-month piece.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yes, both are completed.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But the 77% you said is from 24 into 25?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I stopped you in the middle.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Yes, and so it really depends on the vacancies and the positions that are available and the interest of the candidates.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We do a lot of focus on making sure people are aware of the civil service process, aware and taking civil service exams.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: There may be opportunities that are directly related to the positions that they are interned, they're doing the fellowship with.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So they're able to go into that full-time positions at the agencies.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: For the last program year that ends up where we're at 38%, we know that there are still individuals that are interested and engaged.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: They're currently going through the interview process.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: They may be considering or taking an exam and waiting on a list to be hired.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, so then based on that, I would say it's safe to assume that perhaps more people from the last year could potentially be hired.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, so the 77% is counting people from the 24-25 year who could have still been hired in 2026.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so that could be attributable to the lower number with the 38%.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It just seems like a big drop.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So I'm just trying to figure out.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: 77% seems like a great number.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And a lot of people that moved on into, you know, civil servant work and 38%, not so much.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But if people are still going through the process and.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: People are still going through the process.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how DCAS targets recruitment for technical titles and urgent situations like the Legionnaires outbreak; Porter says they can shift exams and use special hiring events.
chapters.title: Hudson asks about hard-to-recruit specialty titles and urgent situations

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then I just had another question.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Many city positions are vital to the health and well-being of New Yorkers, but require extremely technical and detailed knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: For example,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: For example, the current Legionnaires outbreak may have been exacerbated by staffing shortages for water inspectors, and trained DOB building inspectors are integral to support the city's ambitious housing strategy.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: How does DCAS target its recruitment for hard-to-recruit or specialty titles that require immediate staffing of highly qualified technical experts?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And are there any special processes for urgent situations, such as the Legionnaires outbreak?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Are there methods to expedite accreditation or certification for positions that require such credentials?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So what I will start by saying is that, you know, DCAS, we work in partnership with city agencies to develop our annual examination schedule.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: You know, 80% of the positions that are used across the city requires exams.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So that's first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Our first step with agencies is understanding their immediate hiring needs to ensure that we're developing a recruitment strategy to support their immediate and or future hiring needs.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Can I just ask you there, do those assessments ever change in real time?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So you might do, you know, you might.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Coordinate with or find out from an agency at the beginning of the year what their needs may be, and then you have an outbreak such as this Legionnaires outbreak, and then the needs may change.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: How quickly are you able to shift your recruitment efforts?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We're able to shift immediately.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So immediately meaning we can move an exam.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Later in the exam schedule to give the agent

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: see more flexibility to conduct interview-based hiring, or add an exam to the annual examination schedule and use the applicant pool, for instance, as a recruitment source.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So as folks are applying, we provide that data to agencies so that they can immediately engage with prospective applicants for immediate hiring needs.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We also have the Office of Citywide Recruitment, boots on the ground, that can help amplify immediate hiring needs and also host what we call special hiring events to attract top talent for immediate hiring needs.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So it's really more about agencies communicating their needs to us and us being available to, you know, immediately available to address any hiring needs that they may have.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks if any positions were filled during the outbreaks; Porter says hiring happens at agency level and she will follow up with DOHMH.
chapters.title: Hudson follows up on Legionnaires outbreak and hiring

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you know if either during the summer when the outbreak, when there was an outbreak in the Upper East Side or now as there is one in the South Bronx, there have been any of those positions have been filled?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So we would have to get back to you on exact numbers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Hiring happens at the agency level.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So unless the agency amplifies it to DCAS for support, we would not have insight to like, you know, direct hiring that's happening at the agency level.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you know if DOHMH did that with DCAS?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I would have to take this back.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We can definitely circle back.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: I don't have that information in front of me.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It would be great to know whether or not that happened in real time.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And is currently happening.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks about the minimum qualifications review; Porter says 116 titles reviewed, 69 amended, and the process is ongoing.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about minimum qualifications review

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So we are aware that DCAS has been undertaking a minimum qualifications review of civil service titles in the hopes that some unnecessary eligibility requirements can be eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And as of April 2025, DCAS reviewed 90 titles.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Resulting in amendments to requirements for 61 of those titles, which impacted over 53,000 individual positions.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Have there been more minimum qualification reviews that have been completed since then?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And if so, how many titles have been amended?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How many individual positions do these amendments impact?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: As a quick update, currently we've reviewed about 116 titles, and we've seen a slight increase in expansion, MQR expansions, to about 69 titles.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: This process is ongoing.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We are continuing to review minimum qualification requirements for the titles in the city's title portfolio, and we'll continue to make adjustments where necessary.

chapters.summary: Aldebol notes a drop from 166,000 to 119,117 applications; Porter attributes it to the types of exams offered, like sanitation vs. technical titles.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about decrease in exam applications

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: According to the recently released Mayor's Management Report, in FY26 there were 119,117 applications received for civil service

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: exams compared to 166,000 in fiscal year 25.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: To what does DCAS attribute the decrease in applications?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The application number is a dynamic number.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It's really based on the exams that we're offering for a particular fiscal year.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So for instance, in fiscal years when we're offering a title like sanitation worker, where we receive, you know, 150,000 applications, we'll see,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: you know, an increase, that number would be higher than a year where maybe we're giving more technical titles like engineering or more specialized titles where we see smaller applicant pools.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So, you know, I can give you a more direct answer, but on...

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: You know, in general, that's usually why you see like the fluctuation and examination numbers.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how frequently DCAS hires from lists; Porter explains lists last up to four years and exams are given on 2-3 year cycles, with police exams monthly.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about exam schedule and hiring from lists

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And is that testing schedule is based on the need that the agencies will ask DCAS for?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Yeah, so civil service lists in general, they're usually...

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So long as there are candidates available for up to four years.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So we usually give exams on a two to three year cycle, unless it's a title where there may be an immediate hiring need where we need to give it more often.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So like police officer, we know that the city is in need of police officers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So we give that exam every month.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So we give it 12 times a year.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Whereby a title like sanitation worker, where we have a larger applicant pool, we may give that exam every three to four years.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And how frequently do you actually hire from those lists?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Like, for example, the police officer list.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Yes, so hiring happens at the agency level.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The way it works is that they would contact DCAS when they're ready to hire, and then we would issue them what we call a list certification, which contains the names of candidates who took and passed the examination and are available to be considered for employment.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks about the timeline from exam to hire; Porter says median time from exam to list establishment is 101 days, and hiring depends on agency need.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about time to establish and certify lists

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And generally speaking, how long does it take to establish a list and then certify the list and actually get people hired off the list?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: If we look at the data, right, if we look at the mayor's management report, where we have a metric that measures the time between when we administer an exam to when an exam is established, right now we're under target.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We have a median time of 101 days between exam administration and establishment.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Now, once the list is established,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It would depend upon the agency's, you know, need to hire.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: That would determine how quickly those lists move.

chapters.summary: Aldebol questions the 101-day timeline; Porter explains legally mandated processes like appeals that must be managed before establishing an exam.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks why exams take long to score

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So why does it take so long for exams to be scored?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Because it, you know, 101 business days is quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You know, people are looking for a job.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: They're waiting.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: They take an exam.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: They're waiting.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: It's still a long time, even though there is a decrease from 158 business days.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Yeah, I can definitely explain that.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So there are legally mandated processes that come along with the exam development process, mostly to ensure that, you know, our test takers have the ability to, you know, review and, you know,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: what I'll say is like appeal parts of the process that they may have questions about.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And so by law, we have to set aside certain timeframes to administer those processes.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So in general, that's what takes the most time is those legally mandated aspects of the process that we must

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: manage before we can establish an examination.

chapters.summary: Aldebol notes DOHMH hired quickly for Legionnaires; Porter says DCAS is streamlining and reducing time, with some lists established within 90 days.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about Legionnaires and emergency hiring

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I know that we had a hearing on Legionnaires and DOHMH Commissioner

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: said that

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: They got authorization to hire in November, or they got the budgeted headcount in November, and they were able to hire before.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The summer, which was, I would say, roughly six, seven months, which is a much shorter time frame, still quite long, but a much shorter time frame to get people hired.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: It was, I guess, an emergency situation.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How does that happen?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And we can't seem to do that for other technical titles like that one.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: You know, our goal is to continue to look for ways to streamline and expedite, you know, the hiring process.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And we're doing that through, you know, reviewing our technology and, you know, figuring out ways to move things faster.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: I will say that I'm proud of the DCAS team and how we've been able to reduce the time between exam administration and.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And a list establishment.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In some cases, we're establishing lists within 90 days.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So police officer, we have a standard there where within 120 days, less than 120 days, that list is available to the agency, you know, to hire.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In addition, I would also

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: add that

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: that there are opportunities for agencies to leverage data.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So the data that comes along with the process, the applicant pool, right?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So like at the end of the application period, if an agency has an immediate hiring, immediate need to hire, we can share that information with them to help expedite their recruitment process.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So, you know, we're always looking for ways.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: I will say that there is room for improvement and we're committed to doing so.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks if investigative stage can be done prior to exam; Porter says they are reimagining the process and agencies can hire from published lists before investigations complete.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about investigative stage and exam completion

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah, of the 208 civil service exams that were open for filing in fiscal 2026, 57 of those exams took fewer than 100 days for completion.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The MMR describes that there's a variation in the median completion time due to the types of exams administered.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: With single-part exams being quicker to grade than investigation before appointment exams, which requires the additional investigative stage.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Given the fact that exam grading already takes a significant amount of time, are there ways that the investigative stage could be completed prior to examination?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Or could be done by a different team than the core staff who are tasked with grading the exams?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: That's a great question, and we are looking for ways to reimagine how we manage investigate before appointment titles.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We do recognize that it is

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: a longer timeline.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But once again, that process does not preclude an agency from hiring.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: If they have an immediate hiring need, they can use that published list to hire from until we complete the fuller background investigations.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But we do recognize that it is a very protracted process and we are looking for ways to reduce that timeframe.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks what advice DCAS gives candidates facing long waits; Porter and Otar say they inform candidates of multiple pathways and immediate hire opportunities.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about advice for candidates and expediting process

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Although DCAS has several initiatives that are aimed toward recruiting high-quality candidates, such efforts can be fruitless due to the extended timeline for examination and hire, which in some cases can take well over a year.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Many applicants simply cannot wait for long.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Wait that long for a job offer.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What advice do you share for candidates who are in this difficult position and do you have suggestions for how this recruitment and hiring process can be expedited through removal of bureaucratic hurdles and what bureaucratic hurdles or barriers

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: can realistically be removed to make it faster.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: You know, what I'll say is that we do recognize that the city's hiring process has been, you know, a point of, you know, concern for the general public and, you know, folks who may be looking for employment for some time.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And what I can say here is that, you know, we recognize that and we're.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We're, you know, in talks with our sister agencies, with labor, with the city council to develop new strategies to demystify the civil service, you know, how to engage with the civil service system overall.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And we also have the Office of Citywide Recruitment who, you know, Katie, if you want to share some of the strategies that you folks use to engage and inform.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: The public about civil service.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And thank you.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: One of the things that we make clear is that there's more than one way to get into city government.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We want to make sure that if somebody's taking an exam, then they're taking an exam, but they're not just waiting for the results of that.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We let them know that there are other opportunities to get immediate hire, so they can apply for open vacancies on our website.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: They can participate in, you know, some of our immediate hire events that we hold.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We also, if there is somebody that's qualified for programming, our career pathway programs, and we speak to them about that.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: I think one of the main things is just letting people know the different options that are available to them.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And it's not like a sit and wait.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: It's like, hey, if you start the application process early, if you're in school, you are able to apply for a position or an exam before you graduate.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So we really use that form to make sure that people know what options are available to them.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how many events DCAS held with Veterans Affairs; Otar says she doesn't have the number but they partner on special events like City Talk sessions.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about veterans events

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I want to go back to veterans.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: more underrepresented populations.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How many events did you hold with the Department of Veterans Affairs, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: I don't have that number right now.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We can definitely get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: One of the things that we try to do is to partner on, Katrina mentioned the recent event that we participated in.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We try to do special events like our City Talk sessions where we try to get veterans who are serving in different roles.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Normally we try to look at not just the direct uniform roles that some people envision veterans to go in, but to show a diversity of the work that veterans can do within our city government.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So just spotlight some of the things that they are doing so other individuals can see themselves in the program.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: But I can definitely get, we can get back to you on the total events that we've done with DBS.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks if DCAS recommends specific CUNY courses; Otar says they focus on promoting opportunities and the how-to of getting city jobs, not specific classes.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about Local Law 191 and CUNY courses

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So I want to talk a little bit about past local law implementation.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Pursuant to local law 191 of 2025, DCAS was required to provide materials to CUNY by July 1st of this year to promote careers in civil service.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: These materials include information about civil service process, descriptions of related CUNY programs, and a link to the examination webpage.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Given DCAS's close coordination with CUNY on many civil service pathway initiatives, are there any courses or programs offered at CUNY that you would recommend to civil service applicants writ large to help improve career readiness?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Our engagement with CUNY and the students is more about promoting the opportunities that are available to them, the civil service examinations.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: What we notice is that a lot of people are just not aware of the program.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And then because of the diversity in the jobs that are available for city government, it's hard for us to say, hey, if you take this particular class, then you can apply for city jobs.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: There's a variety of jobs that CUNY students can qualify for, especially with our civil service pathway programs.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: There's about seven different career tracks.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So we focus a lot on giving them the information about how to get into those programs.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We partner with CUNY for CUNY-specific events where we're sharing information about the application process.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We have individuals that have gone through the process speak to them about what that process has been like.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Whenever we're having events, we want to make sure that we make sure that they are invited to participate in those sessions.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And sometimes it could be tied to career readiness where we give them advice on how to participate and how to exceed or excel in the events that we have coming up.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So we may not particularly direct them to a class because of the nature of the jobs within the city, but we focus on information on the how-to when it comes to getting a job in city government.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks which advertising modes are most impactful; Otar says they ask applicants how they heard, but responses may be unreliable and timing delays make it hard to measure.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about Local Law 192 and advertisement impact

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Local Law 192 of 2025 requires DCAST to expand its promotion of civil service exams.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: particularly through LinkNYC, Kia, social media, agency websites, advertisements, TV, radio.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Of these models, of these modes of advertisement, are you able to gather information on which forms of advertisements has been more impactful?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So I guess the question is, when people apply for jobs, do you ask them, how did you hear about this?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Yes, we do have a question on our applications where we ask people how they find out about it.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: But one of the things that with our programming, the timing, it's usually not an immediate response, right?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Because we may provide information about the civil service exams or the jobs, but because of that process, it may be a couple of months later or another year later before we can see the results from those advertisements.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And we do have the opportunity for somebody to say, hey, we heard from it from our social media.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: I mean, there may be opportunities to update that list.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: But normally what we see when people respond to that is going to be the very first thing that's on that list.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: That's what they're going to respond to.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So it's not necessarily a reliable source to show exactly where people are finding out about the jobs or the exams.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I kind of agree or disagree.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: No, I think it's helpful to know what's the most impactful, you know, way of getting information out to people so that you can then prioritize.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: What we're seeing is, let's say if we have a list of people of how people find out about the job.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And number one is like I heard from a colleague.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Sometimes that's what individuals select.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: But we still look and, you know, there's an opportunity for us to go back and see within the last couple of months, what does that look like?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: But we often see that people just gravitate to the first option that's on the list.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how DCAS advertises job fairs; Otar lists newsletters, job board, recruitment page, and community organizations.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about job fairs advertising

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Even for, you know, the job pairs that you hold or anything, do you ask people how they found out about those particular events?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How are you advertising those events?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: For the job fairs that we hold that are specific to a title, we would advertise with our, we have our list of organizations that we work with.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So we'll send them the information.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We have those positions, we have the flyers posted on our job board, as well as there's a decast recruitment page for it.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And then we, you know, create flyers and share it out to our communities and include it in our newsletter.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So there are a variety of ways that we engage with people.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: I'd have to go back and check to see what's been the responses in terms of like how people find out about those specific events.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks about tracking fee waivers; Porter says about 2,000 first-time test takers and 57 high schoolers have requested waivers since July.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about fee waivers tracking

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: In an effort to make the application,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: process less prohibitive, local laws 113 of 2023 and 57 of 2025

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: both focus on providing civil service examination free waivers for justice-involved individuals, high school applicants, first-time applicants.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
