utterances.text: Has DCAS tracked the examinations that such fee waivers were used for and whether there are any trends indicating that fee waivers can be used as a tool to encourage more applicants?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Yeah, we do track the exams for which fee waivers are offered.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: I don't have the information handy here, but what I can tell you is that since implementation in July, about 2,000

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: individuals have requested first-time test taker fee waivers, and 57 high schoolers have requested a fee waiver.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: If it's important, we can get back to you with the exact exams that they requested, those waivers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: That would be helpful.

chapters.summary: Aldebol notes the increase from 48 to 178 events; Otar clarifies it was 95 in FY24 and says they use targeted outreach but can't directly tie events to applications.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about Ambassador Program events and applications

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So on the Civil Service Ambassador Program, in fiscal year 2025, DCAS conducted 178 outreach events that met the Civil Service Ambassador Program requirements,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: which is a huge leap from 48 events that were held in fiscal year 2024.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Have you noticed an increase in applications or attendance at hiring halls or career fairs that corresponds with this increase in outreach events?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: I love this part because I'm excited to speak about the great work that the team does to engage the community.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And so within the Career Pathways team, we try to look at what the needs of the agencies and the needs of the city and where we need to really make more impact and do outreach.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So for fiscal year 2025, we're really focused on increasing our presence across the five boroughs and also working with our educational institutions, both with high schools and colleges.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: I do want to clarify that we had 95 qualifying events in fiscal year 24, not 48.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: But we are trying to use more targeted outreach.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: You know, we are trying to use more targeted outreach to engage the communities and making sure that we are reaching the larger groups.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: From every year, we evaluate how we do outreach.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Sometimes we have to figure out, are there a combination of events that we can have?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Are there different types of events that we can have that will reach a larger population or a larger group, but the same population that we're trying to target throughout the Civil Service Ambassador Program?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And so because of the nature of the program, because of the nature of the communities that we're reaching, we may be speaking to somebody that's in high school that may not be ready to apply for an exam.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: It's hard to specifically tie in an increase in application to an increase in the event that we did for that same year.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks about measurable interest at these locations; Otar says there is interest, especially from justice-impacted individuals who didn't know they could work for the city.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about juvenile justice and foster care events

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: In the 2025 fiscal year, DCAS significantly expanded the locations and settings that Civil Service Ambassador Program events were held in.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: As part of this expansion, there were events held at locations that DCAS had not reached in the past, such as juvenile justice facilities and foster care programs.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Was there a measurable interest in the materials that DCAS was distributing at these locations?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And are you able to share if there are any individuals who submitted applications, if there are any individuals from these groups who submitted applications for civil service exams following these events?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Can you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And maybe a little bit louder.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: I'm hard of hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Was there...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Was there measurable interest in the materials that DCAS was distributing at these locations, such as juvenile justice centers, juvenile justice facilities, and foster care programs?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: I think one of the great things that we see is whenever we go out there to speak to just anyone in the community, it's always like, oh, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Oh, there's an option that's available to us here.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Especially when we engage with the justice impacted individuals, there's this misconception that I can't work for city government if I have, you know, if I'm justice impacted.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And so we see a lot of people, it's just bringing the awareness to them that, hey, there is an opportunity available for you, and here's the process.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And so we continue to engage that community because there continues to be interest in the information that we're sharing.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks if DCAS would provide referrals to CUNY courses for justice-involved youth; Porter says they are supportive and will follow up with sister agencies.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about justice-involved youth and CUNY referrals

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: This council has heard on the justice-impacted community that justice has heard significant concerns

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: from justice-involved youth about critical barriers to education, particularly at secure detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Many young people report that they are not going to school or receiving an education.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: In best cases, youth are given educational packets that receive little to no instruction.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Would DCAS consider providing justice-involved youth with referrals to CUNY courses or career readiness materials to improve their likelihood of entering civil service?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: What I would say is that we're supportive of working with our sister agencies who oversee these facilities to ensure that the

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: justice-involved youth have information readily available to them regarding the civil service system.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So that is something that we can definitely follow up on.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks about the expansion to 400 fellows; Porter says they need to maximize the 400 positions before going back to the state for further expansion.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about Fellowship expansion

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: In August 2026, the Civil Service Pathways Fellowship Program's capacity doubled from 200 to 400 fellows.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What changes does DCAS need to make to accommodate this expansion, and are there plans to expand the fellowship further?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And if so, what are those changes and plans?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So we're very proud of the Civil Service Pathway Fellowship Program.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We have seen tremendous success with administering the program across the city.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: In order for us to expand the program further, it does require us to interact with the state's Civil Service Commission to develop proposals to

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: expand the number and we've been successful.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: This is the third time that we're going back to the state to expand the program.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And so pretty much what they're looking for is that we're maximizing the number of positions that they approved previously.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And so once we get to a, you know, a place where we're fully allocating the 400 positions, we're prepared to go back to the state to continue to increase that number.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: We've been joined by Councilmember Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Good morning, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm going to take a break from asking questions to see if Councilmember Ressler has any questions.

chapters.summary: Restler thanks the chair, notes the need for reform, and asks if there has been a comprehensive review of increasing salaries for hard-to-recruit positions.
chapters.title: Restler introduces himself and asks about hard-to-recruit positions and salary review

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Brilliant.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Aldeball.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This is my first time joining one of your hearings, and it's a pleasure.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: One of my favorite new colleagues here in the Council, and you've been...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Just a tremendous asset and chair of this committee.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I feel like I go to you for questions and guidance on a range of issues, and it's been really helpful, and I really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So thank you for bringing your expertise to the council.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's been a wonderful addition to the body.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Commissioner Porter and team and DCAS.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I had a number of conversations with...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: our amazing new DCAS commissioner at the beginning of her tenure, and she really emphasized that fixing the civil service process is at the top of her priority list.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I really welcome that because we need that prioritization.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We need to do a better job of hiring in city government.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The timelines that it takes right now are simply unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The first question I just wanted to lean in on is around the hard to recruit positions.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We have so many jobs in city government where we fail to fill them consistently over many years, but don't do very much about it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I was recently reading a book that emphasized that when a transit authority

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: hired more engineers, it actually significantly reduced costs on their contracts that they were spending, and that we need to do a better job of building in-house capacity.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know a long-time priority of DC37.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so do more insourcing, not outsourcing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And if we can fill those hard-to-recruit positions, it would make a huge difference.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so I wanted to just ask kind of firstly, has there been a comprehensive review of increasing salaries for hard-to-recruit positions?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And even with an analysis of this,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: savings that that could generate for the city of New York for why we should be increasing these specific positions.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know this is part of an OLR challenge, but I know you're the ones who are really trying to solve it and they're trying to save us money.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So please help us solve it.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So what I can say is that there are many strategies and discussions that are underway to figure out how to modernize the civil service system and make things move faster, building in more transparency and, you know, so that we can better support

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: city agencies in general and the services that they provide.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: As you mentioned, you know, DCAS, we, you know, we're not.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Involved in salary setting per se.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But we can definitely take the question back to, you know, answer if anything is going on.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But from a DCAS perspective...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Are you aware of OLR doing a comprehensive review of hard-to-recruit positions?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Not that I'm...

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Privy to, but there are other things that, you know, other discussions that are underway to figure out, you know, how to modernize the system.

chapters.summary: Restler argues for insourcing and cost savings, and asks about addressing the aging workforce; Porter cites pathway programs and fee waivers as strategies.
chapters.title: Restler follows up on cost savings, insourcing, and aging workforce

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know it's expensive.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It could be potentially, it could seem potentially expensive, but I really think there are cost savings actually in

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: solving for these vacancies and insourcing more that we have to rely on outside consultants because we don't have the capacity.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I really think that DCAS and OLR need to do that comprehensive review.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Relatedly, we had really bad retention data during the Eric Adams administration, and I get it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think a lot of people didn't want to work for Eric Adams and his administration.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For obvious enough reasons.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But the city workforce is continuing to get older and older, as I'm sure you know much better than me.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How are you thinking about addressing the aging workforce, and what are we doing to make sure that we have the next generation ready to take the baton in areas where we're really dependent on the knowledge and expertise of older workers?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: You know, as I mentioned in my testimony, we're invested in attracting young people to city government, utilizing, you know, new modes of operation like social media to get, you know, folks excited about civil service.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We also...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Sending you may out with signs on...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Like our commissioners out there, boots on the ground, making it happen every day.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And, you know, getting us all charged up about, you know, what the future offers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But things like, you know, the pathway programs that we're here talking about, the fee waivers for high schoolers and first-time test takers, expanding internships and apprenticeships.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: These are all things or strategies that we think could help us engage, you know, the next wave of civil servants.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's great.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I think that I love seeing the commissioner out there and with Commissioner Richards and otherwise just trying to bring more people into the city workforce, internship models.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And Chair De La Rosa had, previous chair of this committee, De La Rosa had wonderful legislation that it's great to see this.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: implementing around the internship model.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that, you know, when I have had a chance to read the workforce profile report, which I feel like is always delayed, so I hope, when was the last one released?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We're one fiscal year behind.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And, you know, when I saw you come in, Council Member, I knew you were going to ask about it.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: I know, you were thinking it.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We're working on it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I love the workforce profile report, one of the great reports of city government.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: What it highlights in particular is where we have those gaps of where people are aging out that we need to be recruiting for.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So it's not just recruiting across the board.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's in that targeted way of where do we really need help.

chapters.summary: Restler calls for measuring the entire timeline from exam posting to hiring; Porter says they are in initial stages of tracking but face challenges in a decentralized environment.
chapters.title: Restler asks about global accountability from exam to hiring

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could I do one more question and then I'll shut up?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The last thing I wanted to ask is just,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really feel that DCAS should be measuring itself and we should be holding you all accountable from the time a test is posted until the time somebody is hired.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we need to be thinking about that kind of global life cycle from post, you know, from kind of when,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: from exam to hiring.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I know you're not in control of every step of that process.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I get it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But you are the closest thing we have to, as the deputy commissioner for talent, right?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Like as the person thinking globally about how do we make these systems work better.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I really hope that as you think about the MMR moving forward, as we think about

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: holding ourselves accountable to do a better job at streamlining this process, we can lay out what that timeline looks like from beginning to end because it's not just

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The PC is in DCAS's control.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We need to hold the agencies accountable too.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I know you bring in the HR representatives.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know you do your best to provide guidance and input to help them do their jobs better.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But we should have really good data that shows us that HPD is actually doing a great job with DCAS's help.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: DOHMH is pooping the bed, or whatever it may be.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We need to see that data, and we need to hold ourselves accountable from beginning to end to understand where in the process are we having our greatest obstacles, where are the challenges.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Have you thought about a kind of global accountability from exam posting to hiring dates across the board for how we can do a better job of holding agencies and titles accountable in their hiring of individual titles?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Yes, the short answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We are looking at that.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We're in the initial stages of those conversations.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And it is challenging to track what you're describing only because we work in a decentralized environment.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And there's data that we just don't have access to.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But we agree that that is something that we need to focus on and better track.

chapters.summary: Restler says City Hall must hold agencies accountable and provide data, and thanks the panel.
chapters.title: Restler comments on need for City Hall leadership and thanks

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And this is where we need leadership from City Hall.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know that you guys have the right intentions at DCAS and want to make this work.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But we need City Hall to tell the agencies, you all need to work with them and you need to provide this information.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: When we had sexual harassment issues where DCAS was in the de Blasio administration, where DCAS was that centralized force.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: City Hall said to the agencies, you need to provide this data, you need to work together, and it works.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so we just need that same level of accountability here.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Chair, as always, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really appreciate the chance to go a little bit over, and thank you, Deputy Commissioner Porter.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: team for the chance to ask some questions today.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilman.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks if agencies are siloed; Porter confirms each agency has its own HR and DCAS supports through exams and recruitment.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about agencies being siloed in hiring

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah, on that particular issue of it seems like the agencies are siloed when it comes to hiring.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Yes, each agency is responsible.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: They have their own HR departments, and they're responsible for recruiting and hiring.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And we're here to support them, you know, through examinations and, you know, other methods.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Our small but mighty Office of Citywide Recruitment.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And, you know, just helping them navigate and, you know, to help amplify immediate hiring needs they may have.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So essentially you wait for them to say, hey, we need to hire.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: 20 people in this hard to recruit title.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And then what, you know, what steps do you take to make sure that that happens?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So that's in some instances, there are, you know, many different ways for agencies to recruit and hire.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: There are different title classifications that have different rules and regulations, but the foundation of the city's civil service system

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: are competitive titles that require examination.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And that's why we, you know, administer so many exams.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: a year, on average about 200.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And that's the opportunity for agencies to communicate to DCAS any immediate or future hiring needs that we should be helping them to prepare for.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But in the mix of that,

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: If anything comes up, you know, we're always there to support them by amplifying, by, you know, even hosting special hiring events to help, you know, bring folks into a centralized location and, you know, do on the spot hiring.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So there are many different strategies that we use to support agencies, their HR shops, but exams by far is the cornerstone of the system.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks about the new customer service and community engagement track; Otar says it was created based on agency needs for outreach roles.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about new career track in Fellowship

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So back to the Civil Service Pathways Fellowship.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: In 2026, DCAS added a new career track to the fellowship offerings, which is customer service and community engagement.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about that career track?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So one of the things that we do when we are looking at the programs that we offer and where the city's needs are,

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: and, you know, the Civil Service Pathway Fellowship is one of the ways that we address, like, the hard-to-recruit titles or the areas where we need to have a pathway into those vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And so through conversations with agencies and their needs, we learned that there was a need to have something that is specific to folks that are engaged in outreach, community outreach, community engagement.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And so we worked with our internal partners to make sure that there was an opportunity for individuals who were specifically going to school, are interested in working in those pathways,

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: have an opportunity to participate in the fellowship and eventually, you know, have opportunities to be hired full time into those positions.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks if DCAS tracks fellows who don't pursue city jobs; Otar says they don't currently survey those who leave but will look into it.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about tracking fellows who don't pursue city employment

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And you stated that since the program's launch in 2019, over 75% of fellows that have completed the Civil Service Pathways Fellowship transitioned into full-time employment.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you track separate data that speaks to how many fellows have successfully completed the fellowship but didn't?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: not pursue employment with the city?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And where do you know where those fellows end up?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So we know that for the 78% that participated, that transitioned into a full-time position.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: For those that didn't complete the fellowship, they may have gone into another position across city agencies, or they may have left city government completely.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And so that's one of the things that we are looking at and seeing the retention rate for folks that are interested in continuing their government career.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And we're seeing that number increase as we go through the different cohorts.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And what is the annual attrition rate of the Civil Service Pathways program for this current cohort and previous cohorts?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What percent of fellows finish the program?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And what are the main barriers to completion of the program?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So the way the program is set up, it's a two-year program.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So for the cohort that just started this year, normally the attrition would be, and it's just regular employment, right?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: As you get into a position, there's opportunities for professional development where a person may not be directly aligned with the vacancy that they're in, or the person may choose to self-select out of the program.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So that's where we'll see the transition, where a person may no longer participate in the program.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: But for the programs that have, the cohorts that have completed, we have up to just 76 have transitioned into, 76% have transitioned into a full-time position, where 33%

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: those who are transferred have reached a permanent status.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So it really depends.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: But most of the folks that are participating and complete are going into full-time positions.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks what percentage complete the program; Otar says 76% transition to full-time, and reasons for leaving vary, including fit and other opportunities.
chapters.title: Aldebol follows up on completion percentage and reasons for leaving

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: But my question is a little bit different.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How many of those who enter the program actually come?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What percentage?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: actually complete the program.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I understand that people that complete the program, 76% of them stay in civil service or in public service.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So of course, program completion.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How many, you know, what percentage actually completes the program, finishes the two years?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Yeah, so that's the completion.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So the completion is that the person ended at two years and then they go into full-time positions.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We don't really see folks that complete the program.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: That's the last Senate, right?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: The people that complete the program and then decide, hey, I don't longer want to stay within city government.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So it's going to be roughly the same percentage.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And what do you think almost a quarter of the program completers do not enter city government?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Why do you think the program completers don't, a quarter of them don't enter city government?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you repeat the question for me, please?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Why do you think it's almost a quarter of the program completers do not enter city government?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you have an understanding why?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you survey them?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: It could be for a variety of employment reasons, right?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Sometimes individuals are going into a particular position or working with a particular agency.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So sometimes just like any career move that individuals make, they may decide that this position isn't right for them or

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: because of the employment practices and the needs of the agency, it may be that the person is not ideal for that position.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We don't currently survey the individuals that leave the program.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: That is something that we can definitely look into to find out exactly why it is that they're leaving the program.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how placement is determined if fellows go to a different agency; Otar says they go through normal recruitment process.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about placement in different agencies

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How often do fellows move into full-time city employment in the agency in which they held their fellowship?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Majority of the movements that we have is moving into a full-time position with the agency.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: If fellows elect to pursue employment with a different agency, how is their placement determined?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do they do that on their own?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do they get assistance from the agency, from DCAS?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: If a fellow who completes the program wants to apply for a different vacancy, they'll go through the normal recruitment process where they can apply and interview for that vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And are open roles identified by agencies and approved by OMB prior to the beginning of the fellowship to ensure that all fellows are able to move into full-time employment if they want to?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: That is one of the main criteria of the program.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We want to make sure that there is a full-time vacancy that the person can go into.

chapters.summary: Aldebol notes PSC grew from 106 to 122 interns and 7 to 13 agencies; Otar explains they unified teams and did targeted outreach and expos.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about Public Service Corps expansion

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: With the Public Service Corps program, in FY 2025, 106 PSC interns were placed across seven agencies.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: In FY 2026, 122 PSC interns.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Trending in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Interns were placed across 13 agencies.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What work did DCAS undertake to expand the number of agencies that host interns and to increase the total number of interns?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Yes, and that's the part of the...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You do to amplify that even more.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Yes, that's a part of the exciting work that we do.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So separately, we had within DCAS the Public Service Corps program, internships and fellowship teams, and the recruitment teams were separate under separate units.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And so we brought them under the same umbrella, so that way we can be more strategic in the outreach that we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We can amplify those programs a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Within the Public Service Corps, we really take a look at what our activities were, like our standard operating procedures, and figure out what areas we can improve in.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And then we also did targeted outreach to agencies, to schools.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We had information sessions.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Our team go out to work with the federal work-study individuals at respective schools.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And so we did a lot of the boots-on-the-ground activity to make sure that we were able to bring individuals on.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We also held our public service corps.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Expo.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So twice a year, we gather agencies that are interested in hiring interns, and we bring them in, and they can interview and hire on the spot.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And we saw that that resulted in a lot of interns being hired to grow the program.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you have plans to expand that?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We are celebrating 60 years next month.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And so we are also looking at how we're amplifying how we reach public service core individuals that are qualified for the program and expanding how agencies participate.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So that is one of our main goals that we're working towards this year.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I want to recognize that we've been joined by Council Member Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm going to ask one more question, then I'll turn it over to my colleague to see if she has any questions.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks about future goals; Otar says they are building clear pathways from PSC to Summer Internship to Fellowship.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about future goals for PSC

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What are DCAS's goals for the program in the future?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I see that you have expanded.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you have any specific goals for the future of this program?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So what we're looking at is how do we build a pathways?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So the civil service pathways program directly lead into a full-time position.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We're looking at how do we carry that out for the other programs.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So for a public service core, it could be a short term.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: A person may only be qualified for it because of the federal work study part of it for one semester.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So it worked with them and say, can they go into a

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: a summer internship program, somebody that's participating in a summer internship, can they then come back on as a PSE or later on transfer into, not transfer, but participate in the Civil Service Pathway Fellowship?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So we're trying to build out those clear pathways and educate the individuals that are participating in those programs so they know what pathways they can take if they have a keen interest in staying in city government.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So we're trying to just build that out more robustly.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how many PSC interns entered civil service; Otar says it's difficult to track due to the program's nature and they are focusing on building continuation.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about tracking PSC interns entering civil service

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Over the last five years, how many PSC interns entered into civil service after graduating college?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So that number is a little bit difficult to track just because of the nature of the program.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: As I mentioned, somebody may just be with us for a semester because that's all their grant, allow them to stay, or they may come back and alternate between the timeline.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So we don't really know when they graduate.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We don't really know if they're going to qualify to participate again.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And so that's why we're focusing on how do we build that continuation, where even if they're not participating in Public Service Corps, they still have an opportunity to work for city government in the other programs that we have.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah, is there any thought to figuring out a way to track that?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Because I think it's super important to understand.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The true impact of this program in the long term.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Absolutely.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks if federal opposition to DEI has impacted PSC demographics; Otar says they haven't seen any change and continue to engage qualified individuals.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about federal diversity policies impact

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Has the federal government's opposition to diversity and equity policies impacted the demographics of

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: recent classes of PSC interns and are there any changes to federal work study eligibility surrounding visas and citizenship status that have changed the population of students

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: you are able to take in as part of the PSC program?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: From our viewpoint, we haven't seen any change.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: As you've noticed, we've increased the number of people that are participating in the program, and so we continue to work with the schools to engage those folks that are qualified.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So on our end, we haven't seen any changes.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Turn it over to Councilmember Narcisse if you have any questions.

chapters.summary: Narcisse apologizes for being late due to a union event, then asks how many fee waivers were granted and if the process is simple enough.
chapters.title: Narcisse apologizes for lateness and asks about fee waivers

utterances.text: Good morning and thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you for being here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Usually I'm not late, but I had to apologize for that because 1199 made history today with the city pop workers.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And as a nurse, I feel like it was imperative for me to be present for them.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So that's my apology.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So in civil service, we know we're very much interested around New York City.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's kind of where you can move yourself from poverty to middle class.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So we're very much interested, and I'm sure Chair being actually on point with those questions because we want to make sure everyone has the opportunity to...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Elevate yourself in New York City as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How many exam fees?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Probably you probably ask if I have to repeat your question because

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, I apologize for that too.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How many exempt fee waivers were granted last year?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And is the waiver process simply enough that people actually use it?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Or are applicants paying fees they should not have to before?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So I can get back to you with the actual number of fee waivers that were issued last year, but it's roughly about 25 to 30 percent of the applicants who apply for a civil service exam request the waiver.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: There are many different waivers that are offered.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Veterans, folks who receive Social Security insurance, public assistance.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: If you're unemployed, you can take a free exam.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And most recently, in July of this year, we implemented two new fee waivers as a part of Local Law 57, which offers fee waivers for high school students and first-time test takers.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And so for those two that I just mentioned, the latter, we have seen an increase in use, but it's roughly about 30% of test takers.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks how many veterans credits were applied and how DCAS informs veterans; Porter says credits are in all marketing materials and they work with Veterans Affairs.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about veterans preference credits

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How many veterans preference credits were applied last year?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And how is DCAS making sure veterans know they are eligible?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So the availability of veterans credits, it's embedded in all of our marketing materials.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So it's in our marketing.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Notice of exam.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It's on DCAS's website.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It's in our special circumstances guides.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It's also information that can be amplified through the Department of Veteran Affairs.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So, you know, we make an effort to ensure that all test takers are aware of the many different fee waivers and credits that may be available to them.

chapters.summary: Narcisse suggests DCAS use council members to spread information about veterans' benefits, and thanks them for their support.
chapters.title: Narcisse comments on using council members as allies

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Are you utilizing us as your ally to push?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because I'm very big when it comes to veterans, because you'll be surprised how many veterans in New York City don't know what kind of support they can get still up to now, to today.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So if we can utilize our services, because we each represent different districts, that we can be very helpful to make sure people know.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And thank you, too, because you've been present in my office to support for fair different things that we've been doing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm so appreciative of your service.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks how long it takes from being reached on a list to starting the job; Porter says onboarding happens at agency level and DCAS supports streamlining exams.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about time from list to start and delays

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: After someone is reached on the list.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How long does it take to actually start the job?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Where are the biggest delays, background checks, medical exam, or agency's paperwork?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: You know, at DCAS, we're here to support agency hiring needs through the administration of examination.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And once the scoring process is complete and that exam is ready for agency use, it's really dependent upon the agency's hiring need to request that list.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: From DCAS to start their internal onboarding process.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: You know, we work in a decentralized environment.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So each agency has their own HR department that manages the actual hiring of the candidate.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So, you know, it's kind of difficult for us to like pinpoint exactly where there may be, you know, situations at the agency level.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: But at DCAS, we are working to streamline and expedite the examination process as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: And we're here to support agencies in the event that they have an immediate hiring need where they need DCAS support to either attract candidates and or to support, you know, a streamlined interview process.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We support them in that way.

chapters.summary: Narcisse emphasizes the need to track candidates; Otar says they have exit interview surveys and citywide career counselors to help with retention.
chapters.title: Narcisse comments on tracking and asks about turnover and exit interviews

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The way I see it in my brain, so if I'm sending you folks to work for you, so at least I need to know what's up.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If they're staying, I need to know where they're going and keeping track.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I know it may be difficult, but I'm just thinking.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: Yeah, we track how the agencies are using the actual civil service list, but the onboarding process, that's happening at the agency level.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So the interviewing and the, you know, the issuance of onboarding documentation, the investigative process, all of that happens at the agency level.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Which job have the highest turnover in the first two years?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do you know by any chance?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And what do exit and?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: interviews stay about why the people live because if leaving the agencies or whatever done so we don't I don't have that particular number for you here today but we may be able to provide information about the exit interviews

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: do we have yes for the exit interviews we do have a

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: survey that agencies issue and then we produce a report on it and so a lot of it is sometimes the opportunities to grow within their career or not knowing how to navigate the career

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: in city government after they've landed.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Or just wanting to explore other opportunities outside of city government.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And so one of the things that we have is citywide career counselors, where each agency will have a career counselor,

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: and for anyone that's working in the agency will have access to learning more about how they can progress within their agencies or even across different agencies.

chapters.title: Narcisse thanks DCAS and encourages continued outreach

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And even the unions.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Collaborate, let people know that that just come to volunteer as a union.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: There's other things that are valuable for you in the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Keep on doing it.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'll stop you a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: No, no, no, not at all.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You actually give me a break from asking questions.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how many youth apprentices have enrolled; Porter says DCAS helped create the title but the program is managed by Mayor's Office of Talent and DOE, so they don't have numbers.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about Youth Apprenticeship program enrollment

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: since the Youth Apprenticeship Civil Service title program was announced last November, how many youth apprentices have enrolled?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So the Youth Apprenticeship Program is a great example of how DCAS collaborates with other city agencies to implement pathway programs.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So our main role in the Youth Apprenticeship Program was to help the Mayor's Office of Talent and the Department of Education create the title or the vehicle

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: that is used for that particular program.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So we don't have a direct number for you today because we don't manage the program.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: We just help to implement.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So who manages the program?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: It's a collaboration between the Mayor's Office of Talent and the Department of Education.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So you don't have any sense of what types of apprenticeships they're enrolled in or what apprenticeships are available through the program?

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So what I can say is that the Department of Education taps into their students to participate in the program.

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter

utterances.speaker: Katrina Porter
utterances.text: So if you have anything to add, Katie, and please jump in.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And just that they have several different tracks.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So somebody may be in a project management track or they may be interested in IT.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So within the youth apprentice title, they have different focus areas that they can participate in.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And I know that specifically because I have a couple of them on my team, but they have different tracks that the Department of Education and their partner determine like where the needs are within the city so they can create that track.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So you don't have any data, you don't track the data on this program at all, it's all?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We do not.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how DCAS and SBS advertise career fairs and which agencies participate; Otar says SBS manages events, DCAS amplifies, and many agencies participate.

utterances.text: Collaboration with small business services on hiring halls.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We support in amplifying the information and participating when available.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So we share that information when available in our newsletters.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar

utterances.text: So we'll post it there.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: How can we think about other opportunities for the programs?

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: With SBS, we work with them in a couple of different ways, which we just mentioned with the IRON events.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: We may be there providing information sessions during their actual career fair.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: And then we also work with SBS where we go to the Workforce One Center like eight times a month, whether it's in person or virtually to make sure that we're reaching their population.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
utterances.text: So depending, and I know SBS, very excitingly, they've opened a new job center.

utterances.speaker: Katie Ann Otar
