chapters.summary: Hickey, former NYC Public Schools leader, describes never being trained on civil service, waiting a year for lists, and the difficult rule-of-three hiring process.
chapters.title: Michael Hickey testifies on hiring manager challenges

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: I can go first.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You can go first?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay, perfect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: Thank you, Committee Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: I'm Michael Hickey, Chief of Strategy and Operations for Citizens NYC, but I'm actually here to talk to you about my work as a former leader at the New York City Public Schools, where I helped to start up the community schools team and led the students in temporary housing team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: Yeah, so this is more of my direct experience, lived experience with civil service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: I wanted to start by saying that as a hiring manager overseeing hundreds of personnel, operating with dozens of vacancies at any given moment, I was never trained on how civil service works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: I was never offered an explainer or a tutorial, never invited to a webinar or an onboarding session, was never given a clear point of contact in my own agency or at DCAS or any other city entity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: And everything I learned about civil service, I learned by reverse engineering and crowdsourcing and understanding of this Byzantine and Kafkaesque process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: My team worked with homeless families, helping families get access to food, counseling, school supplies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: It was very complex, specialized, trauma-informed work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: The way a hiring process for our team went was like this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: We would identify a vacancy, a title.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: We would assign headcount and budget.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: And then we'd wait, in my case, a year or more for a list to open up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: We'd wait several more months before the hiring pool began.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: We would sit all day in a room with dozens of other hiring managers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: We would all get to ask one question of an employee, and then we would have to make a decision then and there about whether or not we're going to make an offer to that candidate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: We would be, you know, obviously this rule of three applies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: So either take the warm body that's in front of you, whether they're qualified or not, or you wait until hopefully someone comes along.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: So obviously this is a really difficult, traumatizing process for someone that's trying to work with vulnerable families and feeling constantly like you're unable to meet the needs of those families because you don't have the trained personnel to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: Those are limitations that were clearly set by the process of civil service itself rather than the ability to find candidates.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: Yes, it includes recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: You're welcome.

chapters.summary: Haywood, former DCAS employee, discusses the 2019 hiring assessment, the need for plain language, and the exclusionary nature of the exam process.
chapters.title: Rebecca Haywood testifies on civil service modernization

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: I don't have a hard copy of my testimony, but I will share it after the fact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: My name is Rebecca Haywood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: I'm here today to speak both as a former New York City public servant and as the project lead for DCAS's 2019 citywide hiring assessment as a former DCAS employee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: It was the first comprehensive user-centered review of the city's civil service and hiring process for non-uniform titles, and the work has never been made public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: Today I run an organization where I advise governments nationally on civil service modernization and digital transformation and talk with candidates every day who are trying to get city jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: The issue that we're trying to look at is we're trying to make incremental change to a system that needs an overhaul.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: It makes or breaks the city's ability to deliver key services, and we cannot keep using the same playbook and expecting different results.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: There's a lot of great work going on at DCAS, but there's also, it's a lot of these small incremental changes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: There's a couple of things that I want to highlight that have stuck with me from what we learned talking to over 10,000 prospective employees and current city staff back in 2019.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: about what the true challenges are and how we can address them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: The first is really around information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: We've talked a lot today about it's not a process that people understand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: It uses jargon and language that most New Yorkers cannot talk about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: And we found actually that most city employees who took an exam before they were hired already had a close friend or family member who already worked for the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: It's exclusionary in a different way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: Because the exams are only offered typically once every five years or more, we're seeing lists established for five, six, seven years now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: If you miss your opportunity, you miss out, and the city misses out on a potential highly skilled employee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: Like Mike said,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: staff report learning from their colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: There's a lot of other things, and the last thing I'll hit on is really that we need to be clear about the data and information that we use, how we talk about it in plain language, how we use and provide the data

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: to agencies, to hiring managers, and make sure that things like the list of civil service titles and whether or not you can qualify for them are made available to the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: It's currently only available on the city's intranet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: I have a list of recommendations and other information that I will share via email, but look forward to hearing more about what the council is able to move forward on this topic.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Vaughn of Abundance New York applauds DCAS efforts but calls for updating job titles, cutting evaluation timelines, and publishing time-to-hire data.
chapters.title: Catherine Vaughn testifies on removing bottlenecks

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Aldebar.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: My name is Catherine Vaughn, and I'm the co-founder and co-executive director of Abundance New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: We believe the city can and should make it easier, faster, cheaper, and fairer to build and deliver what New Yorkers want.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And so we push for housing, for more vibrant public transit and public space, for renewable energy, and for more effective government delivery of all of the above.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: We applaud the work the administration and DCAS are doing to expand access to public sector job opportunities from the Ambassadors Program to youth apprenticeships and internships to the recent decision to waive civil service exam fees for high school students and first-time test takers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: We also believe that these measures must be paired with additional reforms to remove bottlenecks and barriers from the entire recruitment and application experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Free civil service exams keep money in applicants'pockets, but the largest cost they face is time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: The months between when exams are offered, or years, the year it takes to get exam results, the months required as hiring managers offer interviews one by one to exam scorers who might no longer be looking for jobs,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: the nine months of unpaid onboarding time between when a provisional offer is made and when an offeree is actually able to start work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: In addition to significant time costs, prospective civil servants face additional barriers to finding meaningful careers within the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Titles and jobs descriptions are outdated and opaque, information on the hiring process is scattered across different websites, and data on different agencies'time to hire is unavailable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: As you review the city's work to recruit,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: diverse talent to its workforce, we urge you to consider the entire application process from soup to nuts and to set ambitious goals around reducing agencies' time to hire and vacancy rates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: We propose a variety of categories, which you can, I'll share my written testimony with you afterward, but

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: first ensure that job titles and descriptions reflect the actual work employees are doing and that these roles, along with hiring process details and exam schedules, are posted in plain language.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Many roles have not had updated descriptions in years or even decades, resulting in such outdated titles as computer associate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Information about which roles require exams is hard to find.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And then I'll just quickly go over.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: I think the second is working aggressively to cut evaluation and hiring timelines as you're questioning really pushed into.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: This could include rethinking when exams are needed, such as for licensed positions where there's already state, you know, stringent state-run licensing processes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And then also, you know, where civil service exams are still appropriate, thinking about how to speed up through continuous recruitment and exam schedules, choosing to deliver exams via structured interview, and moving from the rule of three to banded scoring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And then I'll finally underscore the role of transparency in terms of publishing time to hire across agencies,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: which could both help applicants as they try to get a sense of what they should expect from the process and also identify areas for improvement within and across agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Dujardin of Citizens Union recommends band scoring, removing exam requirements for licensed roles, and publishing expected timelines for exam results.
chapters.title: Amory Dujardin testifies on speeding up hiring

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Alibol and staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: My name is Amory Duchardin, and I'm the Public Policy Manager at Citizens Union.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: A report by the Five Borough Institute at Citizens Union solving the staffing crisis took a deep dive into what City Hall can do to retain and recruit talent, including creative solutions like the programs mentioned here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: We applaud the city for such efforts, but we can go further.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: Taking an exam, applying for that job, going through interviews, receiving an offer, and onboarding often takes over a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: This is not a sustainable recruitment strategy for a modern city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: We must speed up the hiring timeline and make it easier to apply.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: First, adopt band scoring to replace the rule of three.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: When the city hires, it must find three candidates willing to be hired from a ranked list of those who pass the civil service exam, and hiring managers must call through that list in ranked order.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: Calling through can take ages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: Instead, band scoring ranks candidates into tiers such as outstanding, well-qualified, and qualified, and allows managers to choose candidates from the top tier based on fit rather than ranked order.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: Another option is for the city to ask the state civil service commission to remove exam requirements for licensed roles, as Catherine mentioned, where state licensing processes already exist, like for engineers, commercial drivers, or nurses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: Such a change would only require approval from the commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: Additionally, the city should also start being transparent with candidates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: Publish expected timelines for exam results and from hire to start date.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: Find ways to provide other updates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: The city's silence or current silence deters candidates from engaging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: We also need to simplify the application process by establishing plain language standards across all communications and redesigning the civil service and jobs website, an idea that Rebecca mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: Current language is confusing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: It would also help if the city built a tool that lets job seekers search for jobs they are eligible for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: Right now, candidates have the easiest time of applying if they have close friends or family who are civil servants, which creates a problem where only those with insider knowledge apply.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: These are all ideas the city can take now, and we have more if anyone wants to discuss them further.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: I'm happy to try to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I do look forward to working with you all.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I know, Catherine.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You know, it's...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I've been against the one in three rule for a while.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks for actionable ideas; panelists suggest plain language standards, training for hiring managers, sharing candidate pools across agencies, and continuous recruitment.
chapters.title: Chair Aldebol asks public panel what city can implement now without state approval

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I agree that, you know, this is, there are a lot of parts of the system that are antiquated.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: There are some things that we have to go through the state, you know, the state has to make changes and there's some things that we can implement now.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What are some of the things that the city...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And I'll ask anybody, what are some of the things that the city can implement that you think the city can implement now without having to go through the state process?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I also agree on the licensing.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: If people already have to go through a licensing process, why go through the whole process?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Civil service exam process.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I totally agree with a lot of what you have said, but I do want to know from your perspective what the city can do and what we can do as city council to try to move some of these things forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: There's a lot actually that the city can do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: I'll share some and then invite others to join in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: One of the easiest and most straightforward things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: that DCAS can do on its own is really think about the language that it uses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: Introduce and mandate plain language standards that actually get implemented

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: for all sources of information, whether it's going to external applicants, whether it's going to existing city employees, to make sure that every New Yorker understands civil service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: I think if you go to the street right now and ask people what is civil service, most people even walking around this district

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: wouldn't necessarily know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: Another thing that can be done is specifically design materials with hiring managers in mind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: They play an outsized role in bringing staff into the process in partnership with HR.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: It's important to recognize the role that they do play and make sure that they're prepared to participate and understand all of the options available to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: Katrina mentioned some of the social media push and other types of things, which is a great start, but really meeting New Yorkers where they're at through

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: other types of information that isn't self-selecting and things that people see every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: I'll quickly go through a couple others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: We don't have any mechanisms right now for agencies to share strong candidates that apply to one job, particularly non-competitive roles with other agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: We're seeing this come up with the marketing push that was done for

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: the public interest technology, the pit crews at OIT.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: There are hundreds of other technology vacancies that don't get that same level of marketing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: The 4,000 plus candidates for those 35 roles aren't going to be able to be accessed by other agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: So creating mechanisms there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: Others have talked a lot about real timelines, both publishing true hiring timelines and identifying the actual bottlenecks that are holding them up, regardless of agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: And then finally, adopting things like continuous recruitment, band scoring, and alternative evaluation methods like structured interviews when they're appropriate can both maintain the principles of merit and fitness

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Haywood
utterances.text: while speeding up hiring and recognizing that the job market across the city has changed and that city career paths and job availability needs to change along with it.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: Let me just say first that the four of us all know each other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: We've actually spent a lot of time kicking around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: We have a giant spreadsheet, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: And actually went through that to look for ideas that are within the power of the city to enact that have low cost associated with them and that actually in many cases have a way to mitigate the political risks or challenges associated with the changes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: Those are all important variables.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: So the things you're hearing us talk about today reflect some of our thinking about what's actionable by the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: And a lot of it comes down to start with clarification.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: You know, it's a complex process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: Most people don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: I worked for the city for almost 10 years and had to reverse engineer my way into understanding it, like as an investigative journalist, practically.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: So I think we can do a lot to make it more approachable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: Then we can actually begin to have an honest conversation with our entire workforce about what reform would look like and actually have informed advocates who are hiring managers who are part of the process to inform it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: The things that we're talking about today, we believe are common sense solutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: So I'll mention two specifics that Rebecca can call out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: Aligning OMB with the posting authority that's already granted to an agency so that we're not going through another round of approval from OMB for an unnecessary review.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: And that mention of practical civil service training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: for all hiring managers and HR managers across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: I feel like I could design a really, really good training for people to understand in a practical manner what this thing is and how you interact with it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Hickey
utterances.text: I would be more than happy to offer that guidance to my colleagues at DCAS or anywhere else in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: I think Mike and Rebecca have covered a lot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: And as we've mentioned, we would love to, we have a whole spreadsheet on this stuff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: And I think it would take longer than the testimony to go over all those things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: But as they've both mentioned, you know, putting pressure on the mayoral administration to take these actions would be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: Certainly recommended by us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: I also know that there are ongoing contract negotiations, you know, right now between the city and unions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: And one way to tackle a lengthy list like this would be to establish a labor management committee as a result of those contract negotiations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: So, you know, in if in the short time before a contract is probably signed, that can be advocated for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amory Dujardin
utterances.text: We would certainly welcome it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: I don't have much to add beyond what the three of them already said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And we can maybe try to put some of what's in the spreadsheet together and something digestible for your committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: One of our suggestions actually related to the COGE process was to develop

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: once every five years or once every four years of the new mayoral administration, a workforce plan that's kind of similar to the capital planning process that goes into, you know, for each of the agencies, what their five-year outlook is and the, you know, the changing needs of their workforce, which I think also speaks to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: council member wrestlers, questions about kind of an aging workforce and the need to really plan out around turnover.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And then to identify, you know, kind of cross-reference that against data around time to hire and vacancies to identify where do elements of this process need to change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: I think many elements can be changed at the city level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: Certainly there are some laws that would need to change at the state level, but I think, you know, in our spreadsheet, we have many, many rows of, you know, DCAS only, or the administration only could change this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: But I think that part of the issue is the lack of centralized data to really demonstrate where the problems are most severe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And I think also to Council Member Hudson's point,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: you know, like we're the only four people testifying right now, and there might be a few others, but there's, there's, there's not as much of a constituency for this type of change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And yet, we see the direct linkage between

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: vacancies and the time it takes to hire and then the really, really important work done by civil servants on crises and emergencies that are happening in the city, whether it's legionnaires or just getting people cash assistance on time, which we've done kind of a dismal job at.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: And so I think that there's also some work to do to really demonstrate the tie between.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Catherine Vaughn
utterances.text: The experiences that New Yorkers are having that are enabled by government and the bottlenecks and kind of the delays that are written into our policies that are kind of required as part of the process and that don't need to be.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I really appreciate your testimony, and I look forward to getting that spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I mean, it certainly will assist our committee in thinking through what we can do to...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You know, move civil service in a more modern direction, which is something that I think

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: is one of my primary concerns, especially as chair of this committee.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And again, thank you so much for your thoughts and your experiences.

utterances.text: Are there any other...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Folks that want to testify.

utterances.text: Okay, seeing no one else in the chamber.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Is anyone on Zoom?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: No one on Zoom?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So, all right.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So seeing

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: That there is no one going to testify.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Again, I want to remind folks, if you are on Zoom, that you can submit your written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: To testimony at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And we thank the administration and the public for attending this hearing to share your thoughts.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And we look forward to following up on these issues.

utterances.text: With that, the hearing is now adjourned.

summary: Committee on Civil Service and Labor held an oversight hearing on municipal recruitment and civil service pathways.

DCAS testified on programs like the Civil Service Pathways Fellowship, Public Service Corps, and free exams for high school students, while council members questioned hiring delays, vacancy rates, and veterans recruitment.
Public witnesses called for modernizing the civil service system through plain language, band scoring, and publishing time-to-hire data.

topic: Oversight - Municipal Recruitment and Civil Service Pathways
